{{short description|Concept in general relativity and quantum field theory}}
[[File:Stephen Hawking's grave at Westminster Abbey.jpg|thumb|Stephen Hawking's memorial stone at Westminster Abbey, showing his formula for the temperature of a black hole]]
{{Thermodynamics sidebar}}
In [[physics]], '''black hole thermodynamics'''<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Bekenstein |first=Jacob |date=January 1980 |title=Black-Hole Thermodynamics |url=https://physicstoday.aip.org/features/black-hole-thermodynamics |journal=[[Physics Today]] |publisher=American Institute of Physics (AIP) |pages=24–31 |doi=10.1063/1.2913906}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Carlip |first1=S. |year=2014 |title=Black Hole Thermodynamics |journal=International Journal of Modern Physics D |volume=23 |issue=11 |pages=1430023–736 |arxiv=1410.1486 |bibcode=2014IJMPD..2330023C |doi=10.1142/S0218271814300237 |s2cid=119114925}}</ref> is a set of physical relationships between the properties of [[black hole]]s that stands in direct relationship to classical [[laws of thermodynamics]].<ref name="ThroneHawking-1994">{{cite book |last1=Thorne |first1=Kip S. |author-link=Kip Thorne |url= |title=Black Holes and Time Warps: Einstein's Outrageous Legacy |last2= |first2= |publisher=W. W. Norton & Company |isbn=978-0-393-31276-8 |editor-last= |editor-first= |edition= |year=1994|title-link=Black Holes and Time Warps}}</ref>{{rp|442}} The equivalence is developed by replacing [[entropy]] with black hole horizon area and replacing [[temperature]] with black hole horizon surface gravity. Having temperature implies that a black hole must emit radiation, that is, [[Hawking radiation]].<ref name=ThroneHawking-1994/>{{rp|426}}

There is no known way to verify black hole thermodynamics; it is the most widely accepted physical model that combines general relativity, quantum field theory, and thermodynamics,<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Curiel |first=Erik |date=January 8, 2019 |title=The many definitions of a black hole |url=https://www.nature.com/articles/s41550-018-0602-1 |journal=Nature Astronomy |language=en |volume=3 |issue=1 |pages=27–34 |doi=10.1038/s41550-018-0602-1 |issn=2397-3366|arxiv=1808.01507 }}</ref> though Hawking's area law has already been tested by analyzing [[gravitational wave]]s.<ref name=":1">{{Cite journal |last=Mingarelli|first=Chiara M. F.|date=September 10, 2025|title=Landmark Black Hole Test Marks Decade of Gravitational-Wave Discoveries|url=https://physics.aps.org/articles/v18/160|journal=Physics|publisher=American Physical Society (APS)|volume=18|issue=160}}</ref>

== History ==
In 1972, [[Jacob Bekenstein]] conjectured that black holes should have an entropy proportional to the area of the event horizon,<ref>{{cite journal |last1 = Bekenstein |first1 = A. |title =  Black holes and the second law |journal =  Lettere al Nuovo Cimento |volume = 4 |pages = 99–104 |year = 1972 |issue = 15 |doi =10.1007/BF02757029 |s2cid = 120254309}}</ref> where by the same year, he proposed the no-hair theorem. In 1973 Bekenstein heuristically suggested <math>\frac{\ln{2}}{8\ \!\pi}\approx 0.0276</math> as the constant of proportionality.<ref name="Bekenstein1973">{{cite journal |last=Bekenstein |first=Jacob D. |title=Black Holes and Entropy |journal=Physical Review D |volume=7 |issue=8 |pages=2333–2346 |date=1973-04-15 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevD.7.2333}}</ref> The next year, in 1974, [[Stephen Hawking]] showed that black holes emit thermal Hawking radiation<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Hawking |first=Stephen |date=March 1, 1974 |title=Black Hole Explosions? |url=https://www.nature.com/articles/248030a0 |journal=Nature |volume=248 |issue=5443 |pages=30–31 |bibcode=1974Natur.248...30H |doi=10.1038/248030a0 |s2cid=4290107 |url-access=subscription}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.technologyreview.com/2010/09/27/200255/first-observation-of-hawking-radiation/ |date=September 27, 2010 |title=First Observation of Hawking Radiation |url-status=live |archive-url=<!--Old URL, same content-->https://web.archive.org/web/20120301205626/http://www.technologyreview.com/blog/arxiv/25805/ |archive-date=2012-03-01 |website=[[Technology Review]] |access-date=17 September 2025}}</ref><ref>{{cite magazine |last=Matson |first=John |title=Artificial event horizon emits laboratory analogue to theoretical black hole radiation |magazine=Scientific American |date=October 1, 2010 |url=http://www.scientificamerican.com/article.cfm?id=hawking-radiation }}</ref> corresponding to a certain temperature (Hawking temperature).<ref>{{cite book |title=[[A Brief History of Time]] |first=Stephen |last=Hawking |publisher=Bantam |year=1988}}</ref> Using the [[thermodynamic]] relationship between energy, temperature and entropy, Hawking was able to confirm Bekenstein's conjecture and fix the constant of proportionality at <math>1/4</math>:<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Hawking |first1=Stephen W. |year=1975 |title=Particle creation by black holes |url=http://projecteuclid.org/euclid.cmp/1103899181 |journal=Communications in Mathematical Physics |volume=43 |issue=3 |pages=199–220 |bibcode=1975CMaPh..43..199H |doi=10.1007/BF02345020 |s2cid=55539246}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |first = Parthasarathi |last = Majumdar |title = Black Hole Entropy and Quantum Gravity |arxiv = gr-qc/9807045 |journal = Indian Journal of Physics |year = 1999 |bibcode = 1999InJPB..73..147M |volume = 73.21 |issue = 2 |page = 147 }}</ref>

<math display="block">S_\text{BH} = \frac{k_\text{B} A}{4 {\ell_\text{P}}^2},</math>

where <math>A</math> is the area of the event horizon, <math>k_\text{B}</math> is the [[Boltzmann constant]], and <math>\ell_\text{P} = \sqrt{G\hbar / c^3}</math> is the [[Planck length]].

{{anchor|Bekenstein–Hawking formula}}<!--different dashes-->{{anchor|Bekenstein-Hawking formula}}This is often referred to as the '''Bekenstein–Hawking formula'''<!--boldface per WP:R#PLA-->. The subscript ''BH'' either stands for ''black hole'' or ''Bekenstein–Hawking''. The fact that the black hole entropy is also the maximal entropy that can be obtained by the [[Bekenstein bound]] (wherein the Bekenstein bound becomes an equality) was the main observation that led to the [[holographic principle]].<ref name="Bousso 2002 825–874" /> This area relationship was generalized to arbitrary regions via the [[Ryu–Takayanagi conjecture|Ryu–Takayanagi formula]], which relates the [[entanglement entropy]] of a [[boundary conformal field theory]] to a specific surface in its dual gravitational theory.<ref name="vr">
{{cite book
 | last1 = Van Raamsdonk |first1 = Mark
 | title = New Frontiers in Fields and Strings
 | pages = 297–351
 | chapter = Lectures on Gravity and Entanglement
 | date = 31 August 2016
 | arxiv = 1609.00026
 | doi = 10.1142/9789813149441_0005
 | isbn = 978-981-314-943-4
 | s2cid = 119273886
 }}</ref>

In the early 1990s [[Gerard 't Hooft]] and [[Leonard Susskind]] generalized the relationship between a black hole's surface area and its entropy, applying to all of spacetime. This was an early form of the [[holographic principle]], a universal relationship between geometry and information. The idea is that the area surrounding any volume in spacetime limits the information content of the volume. Thus the number of degrees of freedom in any volume is bounded and not infinite.<ref name="Bousso 2002 825–874">{{cite journal |last=Bousso |first=Raphael |year=2002 |title=The Holographic Principle |journal=[[Reviews of Modern Physics]] |volume=74 |issue=3 |pages=825–874 |doi=10.1103/RevModPhys.74.825 |arxiv=hep-th/0203101 |bibcode=2002RvMP...74..825B|s2cid=55096624 }}</ref>

Although Hawking's calculations gave further thermodynamic evidence for black hole entropy, until 1995 no one was able to make a controlled calculation of black hole entropy based on [[statistical mechanics]], which associates entropy with a large number of [[Microstate (statistical mechanics)|microstates]]. Some work, called no-hair theorems,<ref name="arxiv.org">{{cite journal |arxiv=gr-qc/0702006 |bibcode=2007PhRvL..99t1101B |doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.99.201101 |pmid=18233129 |title=Black-Hole No-Hair Theorems for a Positive Cosmological Constant |journal=Physical Review Letters |year=2007 |volume=99 |issue=20 |article-number=201101 |first=Sourav |last=Bhattacharya|s2cid=119496541 }}</ref> suggested that black holes could have only a single microstate. The situation changed in 1995 when [[Andrew Strominger]] and [[Cumrun Vafa]] calculated<ref>{{cite journal |last1 = Strominger |first1 = A. |last2 = Vafa |first2 = C. |title = Microscopic origin of the Bekenstein–Hawking entropy |journal = Physics Letters B |volume = 379 |issue = 1–4 |pages = 99–104 |year = 1996 |doi = 10.1016/0370-2693(96)00345-0|arxiv = hep-th/9601029 |bibcode = 1996PhLB..379...99S |s2cid = 1041890 }}</ref> the Bekenstein–Hawking entropy of a [[supersymmetry|supersymmetric]] black hole in [[string theory]], using methods based on [[D-branes]] and [[string duality]]. Their calculation was followed by many similar computations of entropy of large classes of other [[extremal black hole|extremal]] and [[near-extremal black hole]]s, and the result always agreed with the Bekenstein–Hawking formula. However, for the [[Schwarzschild black hole]], viewed as the furthest-from-extremal black hole, the relationship between micro- and macrostates has not been characterized. Efforts to develop an adequate answer within the framework of string theory continue.{{As of?|date=September 2025}}

In [[loop quantum gravity]] (LQG) it is possible to associate a geometrical interpretation with the microstates: these are the quantum geometries of the horizon. LQG offers a geometric explanation of the finiteness of the entropy and of the proportionality of the area of the horizon.<ref name="Rovelli1996">{{cite journal |last=Rovelli |first=Carlo |year=1996 |title=Black Hole Entropy from Loop Quantum Gravity|journal=Physical Review Letters |volume=77 |issue= 16|pages=3288–3291 |doi=  10.1103/PhysRevLett.77.3288|pmid=10062183 |arxiv=gr-qc/9603063 |bibcode=  1996PhRvL..77.3288R|s2cid=43493308 }}</ref><ref name="Ashtekar1997">{{cite journal |last=Ashtekar |first=Abhay |last2=Baez |first2=John |last3=Corichi |first3=Alejandro |last4=Krasnov |first4=Kirill |year=1998 |title=Quantum Geometry and Black Hole Entropy |journal=Physical Review Letters |volume=80 |issue=5 |pages=904–907 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.80.904 |arxiv=gr-qc/9710007 |bibcode=1998PhRvL..80..904A|s2cid=18980849 }}</ref> It is possible to derive, from the covariant formulation of full quantum theory ([[spin foam]]), the correct relation between energy and area (first law), the [[Unruh temperature]] and the distribution that yields Hawking entropy.<ref name="Bianchi2012">{{cite arXiv |last=Bianchi |first=Eugenio |year=2012 |title=Entropy of Non-Extremal Black Holes from Loop Gravity |eprint=1204.5122 |class=gr-qc }}</ref> The calculation makes use of the notion of [[dynamical horizon]] and is done for non-extremal black holes. There seems to be also discussed the calculation of Bekenstein–Hawking entropy from the point of view of LQG. The current accepted microstate ensemble for black holes is the [[microcanonical ensemble]]. The partition function for black holes results in a negative [[heat capacity]]. In canonical ensembles, there is limitation for a positive heat capacity, whereas microcanonical ensembles can exist at a negative heat capacity.<ref>{{cite journal |last1 = Casadio |first1 = R. |title =  Microcanonical description of (micro) black holes |journal = Entropy |year = 2011 |volume = 13 |issue = 2 |pages = 502–517 |s2cid = 120254309 |doi=10.3390/e13020502 |arxiv = 1101.1384 |bibcode = 2011Entrp..13..502C |doi-access = free }}</ref>

Analyses of gravitational waves emitted by [[GW250114]] confirmed Hawking's assertion that the surface area of a black hole is a non-decreasing function of time.<ref name="Abac-testing2">{{cite journal |last1=Abac|first1=A.G.|date=September 10, 2025|title=GW250114: Testing Hawking's Area Law and the Kerr Nature of Black Holes|journal=[[Physical Review Letters]]|volume=135|issue=11|article-number=111403|doi=10.1103/kw5g-d732|doi-access=free|arxiv=2509.08054|last2=Abouelfettouh|first2=I.|display-authors=1}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|title=Black Hole Spectroscopy and Tests of General Relativity with GW250114|last=Abac|first=Adrian|date=29 January 2026|journal=Physical Review Letters|issue=136|page=041403|last2=Abouelfettouh|first2=I.|display-authors=1|url=https://journals.aps.org/prl/abstract/10.1103/6c61-fm1n|doi=10.1103/6c61-fm1n|hdl=10261/427936|hdl-access=free}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|url=https://physics.aps.org/articles/v19/s2|title=General Relativity Survives a Tough Trial|last=Wilkinson|first=Ryan|date=29 January 2026|journal=[[Physics (magazine)|Physics]]|issue=2|volume=19|publisher=American Physical Society}}</ref>

== Laws of classical black hole mechanics ==
These four '''laws of black hole mechanics''' are relationships between physical properties of [[black hole]]s assuming general relativity but no quantum effects. This form is analogous to the laws of thermodynamics but without quantum effects the black hole temperature must be zero and simply absorbs all radiation.<ref name=Carlip-2017>{{Citation |last=Carlip |first=S. |title=Black hole thermodynamics |date=July 2017 |pages=415–465 |url=https://www.worldscientific.com/doi/abs/10.1142/9789814678506_0010 |access-date=2026-01-03 |doi=10.1142/9789814678506_0010|doi-access=free }}</ref> This is the form proposed by Bardeen, [[Brandon Carter]], and Hawking in 1973<ref>{{cite journal |last=Bardeen |first=J. M. |author2=Carter, B. |author3=Hawking, S. W.  |year=1973 |title=The four laws of black hole mechanics |journal=Communications in Mathematical Physics |volume=31 |issue=2 |pages=161–170 |doi=10.1007/BF01645742 |bibcode = 1973CMaPh..31..161B |s2cid=54690354 |url=http://projecteuclid.org/euclid.cmp/1103858973 }}</ref> (expressed in [[geometrized units]]).

=== Zeroth law ===
For a stationary black hole (one in [[mechanical equilibrium]])<ref name=WaldLiving/>{{rp|10}}
the [[surface gravity]], <math>\kappa</math>, is constant on the event horizon. This is the analog of the [[zeroth law of thermodynamics]] on the equivalence of temperature across a system at equilibrium with surface gravity being analogous to temperature.<ref name=Carlip-2017/>{{rp|417}}

=== First law ===
For perturbations of stationary black holes, the change of energy is related to change of area, angular momentum, and electric charge by

<math display="block">dE = \frac{\kappa}{8\pi}\,dA + \Omega\,dJ + \Phi\,dQ,</math>

where <math>E</math> is the [[energy]], <math>\kappa</math> is the surface gravity, <math>A</math> is the horizon area, <math>\Omega</math> is the [[angular velocity]], <math>J</math> is the [[angular momentum]], <math>\Phi</math> is the [[Electric potential|electrostatic potential]] and <math>Q</math> is the [[electric charge]].  Analogously, the [[first law of thermodynamics]] is a statement of [[conservation of energy|energy conservation]], which contains on its right side a term equal to temperature times change in entropy, <math>T dS</math>.

=== Second law ===

The horizon area is, assuming the [[Energy condition#Mathematical statement|weak energy condition]], a non-decreasing function of time:

<math display="block">\frac{dA}{dt} \geq 0.</math>
Here black hole surface area is analogous to thermodynamic entropy and the laws say these properties can never spontaneously decrease.<ref name=WaldLiving/>{{rp|6}}

=== Third law ===

It is not possible to form a black hole with vanishing surface gravity. That is, <math>\kappa = 0</math> cannot be achieved.
This is analogous to some but not all forms of the [[third law of thermodynamics]].<ref name=WaldLiving/>{{rp|10}}

=== Quantum effects ===

The generalized second law of thermodynamics (GSL) is needed to present the second law of thermodynamics as valid. This is because the second law of thermodynamics, as a result of the disappearance of entropy near the exterior of black holes, is not useful. The GSL allows for the application of the law because it allows for the measurement of interior, common entropy. The validity of the GSL can be established by studying an example, such as looking at a system having entropy that falls into a bigger, non-moving black hole, and establishing upper and lower entropy bounds for the increase in the black hole entropy and entropy of the system, respectively.<ref name="Bekenstein1974">{{cite journal |last=Bekenstein |first=Jacob D. |date=1974-06-15 |title=Generalized second law of thermodynamics in black hole physics |journal=Physical Review D |volume=9 |issue=12 |pages=3292–3300 |doi=10.1103/physrevd.9.3292 |issn=0556-2821 |bibcode=1974PhRvD...9.3292B|s2cid=123043135 }}</ref> The GSL also holds for theories of gravity such as [[general relativity]], [[Lovelock theory of gravity|Lovelock gravity]], or [[braneworld]] gravity, because the conditions to use it for these theories can be met.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Wu|last2=Wang|last3=Yang|last4=Zhang|first=Shao-Feng|first2=Bin|first3=Guo-Hang|first4=Peng-Ming|date=17 November 2008|title=The generalized second law of thermodynamics in generalized gravity theories|journal=Classical and Quantum Gravity|volume=25|issue=23|article-number=235018|doi=10.1088/0264-9381/25/23/235018|arxiv=0801.2688|bibcode=2008CQGra..25w5018W|s2cid=119117894}}</ref>

However, on the topic of black hole formation, the question becomes whether or not the generalized second law of thermodynamics will be valid, and if it is, it will have been proved valid for all situations. Because black hole formation is not a stationary event, proving that the GSL holds is difficult. Proving it is generally valid would require [[Quantum statistical mechanics|quantum-statistical mechanics]], because the GSL is both a [[Quantum laws|quantum]] and [[Empirical statistical laws|statistical law]]. This discipline does not exist{{clarify|date=September 2025}} so the GSL can be assumed to be useful in general, as well as for prediction. For example, one can use the GSL to predict that, for a cold, non-rotating assembly of <math>N</math> [[nucleons]], <math>S_\text{BH} - S > 0</math>, where <math>S_\text{BH}</math> is the entropy of a black hole and <math>S</math> is the sum of the ordinary entropy.<ref name="Bekenstein1974" /><ref name=WaldLiving>{{cite journal |last=Wald |first=Robert M. |date=2001 |title=The Thermodynamics of Black Holes |journal=Living Reviews in Relativity |volume=4 |issue=1 |article-number=6 |doi=10.12942/lrr-2001-6 |doi-access=free |issn=1433-8351 |pmc=5253844 |pmid=28163633 |arxiv=gr-qc/9912119 |bibcode=2001LRR.....4....6W }}</ref>

==== Third law ====
The third law of black hole thermodynamics is controversial.<ref name=Racz2000>{{cite journal |last=Rácz |first=István |date=2000-10-21 |title=Does the third law of black hole thermodynamics really have a serious failure? |url=https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/0264-9381/17/20/410 |journal=Classical and Quantum Gravity |volume=17 |issue=20 |pages=4353–4356 |doi=10.1088/0264-9381/17/20/410 |issn=0264-9381|arxiv=gr-qc/0009049 }}</ref> Specific counterexamples called [[extremal black hole]]s fail to obey the rule.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Wald |first=Robert M. |date=1999-12-01 |title=Gravitation, thermodynamics and quantum theory |url=https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/0264-9381/16/12A/309 |journal=Classical and Quantum Gravity |volume=16 |issue=12A |pages=A177–A190 |arxiv=gr-qc/9901033 |bibcode=1999CQGra..16A.177W |doi=10.1088/0264-9381/16/12A/309 |issn=0264-9381 }}</ref> The classical third law of thermodynamics, or [[Nernst's theorem]], which says the entropy of a system must go to zero as the temperature goes to absolute zero, is also not a universal law.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Wald |first=Robert M. |date=1997-11-15 |title='Nernst theorem' and black hole thermodynamics |url=https://link.aps.org/doi/10.1103/PhysRevD.56.6467 |journal=Physical Review D |language=en |volume=56 |issue=10 |pages=6467–6474 |arxiv=gr-qc/9704008 |bibcode=1997PhRvD..56.6467W |doi=10.1103/PhysRevD.56.6467 |issn=0556-2821 }}</ref> However, systems that fail the classical third law have not been realized in practice, leading to the suggestion that the extremal black holes may not represent the physics of black holes generally.<ref name=Racz2000/>

A weaker form of the classical third law known as the ''unattainability principle''<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Masanes |first1=Lluís |last2=Oppenheim |first2=Jonathan |date=2017-03-14 |title=A general derivation and quantification of the third law of thermodynamics |journal=Nature Communications |language=en |volume=8 |issue=1 |article-number=14538 |doi=10.1038/ncomms14538  |doi-access=free|issn=2041-1723 |pmc=5355879 |pmid=28290452|arxiv=1412.3828 |bibcode=2017NatCo...814538M }}</ref> states that an infinite number of steps are required to put a system into its [[ground state]]. This form of the third law does have an analog in black hole physics.<ref name=WaldLiving/>{{rp|10}}

=== Interpretation of the laws ===
The four laws of black hole mechanics suggest that one should identify the surface gravity of a black hole with temperature and the area of the event horizon with entropy, at least up to some multiplicative constants. If black holes are only considered classically, then they have zero temperature, and by the [[no-hair theorem]],<ref name="arxiv.org"/> zero entropy, and the laws of black hole mechanics remain an analogy. However, when quantum-mechanical effects are taken into account, it is found that black holes emit [[thermal radiation]] (Hawking radiation) at the Hawking temperature<ref name=WaldLiving/>{{rp|12}}

<math display="block">T_\text{H} = \frac{\kappa}{2\pi}.</math>

From the first law of black hole mechanics, this determines the multiplicative constant of the Bekenstein–Hawking entropy, which is (in [[geometrized units]])

<math display="block">S_\text{BH} = \frac{A}{4}.</math>

which is the entropy of the black hole in Einstein's [[general relativity]]. [[Quantum field theory in curved spacetime]] can be utilized to calculate the entropy for a black hole in any covariant theory for gravity, known as the Wald entropy.<ref name="WaldLiving" />

== Critique ==
While black hole thermodynamics (BHT) has been regarded as one of the deepest clues to a quantum theory of gravity, there remains criticism that "the analogy is not nearly as good as is commonly supposed", that it "is often based on a kind of caricature of thermodynamics" and "it's unclear what the systems in BHT are supposed to be".<ref name="dougherty callendar">{{cite web |author1=Dougherty, John |author2=Callender, Craig |title=Black Hole Thermodynamics: More Than an Analogy? |url=http://philsci-archive.pitt.edu/13195/1/bht.pdf |website=philsci-archive.pitt.edu |publisher=Guide to the Philosophy of Cosmology, editors: A. Ijjas and B. Loewer. Oxford University Press }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last1=Foster |first1=Brendan Z. |title=Are We All Wrong About Black Holes? Craig Callender worries that the analogy between black holes and thermodynamics has been stretched too far |url=https://www.quantamagazine.org/craig-callender-are-we-all-wrong-about-black-holes-20190905/ |website=quantamagazine.org |access-date=3 September 2021 |date=September 2019 }}</ref>

Others have come to the opposite conclusion believing, "stationary black holes are not ''analogous'' to thermodynamic systems: they ''are'' thermodynamic systems, in the fullest sense."<ref name="wallace 2018">{{cite journal |last1=Wallace |first1=David |title=The case for black hole thermodynamics part I: Phenomenological thermodynamics |journal=Studies in History and Philosophy of Science Part B: Studies in History and Philosophy of Modern Physics |publisher=Philosophy of Modern Physics, Volume 64, Pages 52-67 |doi=10.1016/j.shpsb.2018.05.002 |date=November 2018|volume=64 |pages=52–67 |arxiv=1710.02724 |bibcode=2018SHPMP..64...52W |s2cid=73706680 }}</ref>
